transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I guess… I don’t feel like myself anymore. I’ve gotten real quiet, like I don’t have much to say to anybody, even when people at work try to talk. I just kind of go flat.

And getting started on my cleaning route, it feels way harder than it should—like pushing one of those heavy carts when the wheel’s stuck. I used to just do it, you know, go floor to floor… but now I just stand there sometimes. It’s not like the old days when the building had those waxed floors that smelled real strong—sorry, I’m getting off track. I just… I’m not acting like me.
How long have you been feeling this way, like you’re not acting like yourself?

It’s been… I think about a year and five months now. It kind of started after I had to leave my old apartment, my old neighborhood. I still think about that place sometimes—the corner store, the bus stop with the busted sign—and I guess after that, things just kept building up. So yeah… around a year and five months.
Have you noticed that things you used to enjoy, like your work or other activities, don’t interest you as much anymore?

Yeah… yeah, I have. I used to look forward to Saturdays, going fishing if the weather wasn’t too bad. I’d get the coffee ready early, sometimes do a crossword before heading out—there was this one pen I liked, wrote real smooth, don’t know where it went now.

And at work, I used to like showing the younger guys little tricks, like how to strip a floor without making a mess of it. That used to feel… I don’t know, useful. Now I mostly just let all that sit. Fishing stuff, crosswords, even work things… they don’t really give me anything back anymore.
Can you tell me more about how you feel when you try to do those things now—like fishing or helping the younger guys at work? Do they make you feel anything, or do they just feel empty?

Mostly they feel… empty, I guess. Like I’ll think, “Saturday, maybe I should go fishing,” and then the rods just stay where they are. I used to get coffee going early, sit with a crossword a bit—there was this mug I always used, chipped on the side but it held heat good—and then I’d head out.

Now it’s like none of it gives me that little pull anymore. Same at work. I used to like showing the younger guys how to strip a floor right, how not to flood the corners and make a big mess. That used to make me feel useful. Now I mostly just let it sit, let somebody else say something if they want. It doesn’t really give me anything back.
Do you feel down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day?

I don’t know if I’d say most of the day… I mean, some days I wake up and it’s like the whole room feels heavy, you know? But then I’ll get distracted by something stupid, like the radiator making that clicking sound or a guy outside backing up his truck for ten minutes.

So… depressed, yeah, I guess sometimes. Nearly every day, I’m not sure. I don’t keep track of it like that. It kind of comes and goes, but there’s a lot of days where it’s just sitting there.
Do you find that you feel tired or lack energy a lot of the time, even when you haven't done much?

Yeah… I do. Even if I sleep through the night, which you’d think would help, by the time I get to the building my arms and legs feel like they’ve got weights on ’em.

It’s not even always big stuff. Hauling trash bags, changing liners, little jobs I used to just do without thinking—now they wear me out more than they should. Sometimes I’ll stand there a minute by the supply closet, you know, where the mop heads hang… they never dry right if people bunch ’em up. But yeah, mostly I just feel tired before I’ve really done much.
Have you found yourself feeling like you're not worth much or that you're failing at things more often than not?

Yeah… I do get that. More than I like to say.

I keep thinking I messed things up, you know, losing my old place and not keeping my life together the way a grown man’s supposed to. And then it spreads out from there, like if the church pantry is short on something, I start thinking maybe I should’ve done more, even if that don’t make much sense. Or if a hallway gets missed at work, even if it wasn’t my section exactly, it feels like somehow that’s on me too.

It’s stupid maybe, but it sits there. Like I failed people. Like I should’ve been able to keep everything from falling apart.
Would you say that most days, your mood stays down most of the day, like a constant weight that doesn’t really lift?

It’s been… yeah, a long stretch. I don’t know if every single day is the same, but that low part’s been around since not too long after I moved.

That move—boxes everywhere, and I remember I couldn’t find the coffee filters for like a week, which shouldn’t matter, but it did. Anyway… I’d say it’s been about a year and a couple months now that it’s been hanging over me. Not always the exact same weight, but it hasn’t really gone away.
Is there anything at all that you still enjoy—something that gives you even a little pleasure—or has that completely gone away?

I mean… not completely gone, I guess, but it’s close.

I used to really look forward to Saturdays, going fishing if the weather was decent. I had this old tackle box—hinge sticks on one side—and I’d mess with the lures more than I needed to. Now I mostly just let it sit. Same with crosswords and coffee in the morning. I used to like that, felt like it got my head moving a little, but now I’ll open the paper and just… leave it there.

Even at work, showing the younger guys little tricks, like how to strip a floor without making a bigger mess than you started with—I used to get something out of that. Now it just feels like another thing. Doesn’t really give me much back anymore.

Can you tell me if you’ve completely stopped doing things you used to enjoy, like fishing or working with the younger guys at work, or do you still try to do them sometimes even if they don’t feel the same?

I haven’t completely stopped, no… I mean, the fishing pole’s still there, and sometimes I’ll think, “Maybe Saturday,” but then Saturday comes and I just don’t go. The tackle box just sits there. Same with the crosswords—I’ll have the coffee, open the paper, and then it’s like the words don’t matter much.

At work, if one of the younger guys asks me something, I’ll still show him, like with stripping a floor right so you don’t make a bigger mess. I can do it. I just don’t get that little good feeling from it like I used to. It’s more like… I’m going through the motions. Those things used to give me something back, and now mostly they don’t.
Would you say that you’ve lost all or almost all pleasure in all activities you used to enjoy, not just most of them?

Yeah… almost all, I’d say. Not every single second, I guess, but the things I used to count on don’t really give me anything back now.

Fishing on Saturdays used to be the big one. I’d get the gear ready, check the line, fuss with the tackle box—there’s a little tray in there that never sits right—and now I mostly just leave it where it is. Same with the crossword and coffee. I’ll sit there with the paper, and it’s like I’m looking at it but not really getting anything from it.

Even showing the younger guys at work how to strip a floor the right way… I used to feel useful doing that. Now I can still do it, but it’s flat. So, yeah, I’d say it’s close to all of it.
